n:
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Get up!”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “this Jordan”; the word “River” has been supplied in the translation for clarity (likewise in v. {{Joshua 1:11|11}}).

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “Cross over this Jordan, you and all these people, to the land that I am giving to them, to the children of Israel.” The final phrase, “to the children of Israel,” is probably a later scribal addition specifying the identity of “these people/them.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Every place on which the sole of your foot walks, to you I have given it, as I said to Moses.” The second person pronouns in vv. {{Joshua 1:3|3-4}} are plural, indicating that all the people are addressed here. The verbal form נְתַתִּיו (netattiv, “I have given it”) is probably a perfect of certitude, emphasizing the certainty of the action. Another option is to translate, “I have already assigned it.” In this case the verb would probably refer to the Lord’s decree to Abraham that he would give this land to his descendants.

*Translator's note:* A מִדְבָּר (midbar, “wilderness, desert”) refers to a dry region which is characterized by receiving less than twelve inches of rain per year. It therefore cannot support trees, yet may have sparse vegetation if it receives more than six inches of rain. If it receives less than six inches, then “desert” is an appropriate term (usually not a sandy desert). Most cases of the term are rendered as “wilderness” in NET. Here it refers to the southern border of the nation which stretches down into Sinai.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all the land of the Hittites.” The expression “the land of the Hittites” does not refer to Anatolia (modern Turkey), where the ancient Hittite kingdom of the second millennium b.c. was located, but rather to Syria, the “Hatti land” mentioned in inscriptions of the first millennium b.c. (see *HALOT* 363-64 s.v. חִתִּי). The phrase is omitted in the LXX and may be a scribal addition.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the Great Sea,” the typical designation for the Mediterranean Sea.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “From the wilderness and this Lebanon even to the great river, the River Euphrates, all the land of the Hittites, even to the great sea [at] the place where the sun sets, your territory will be.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “A man will not stand before you.” The second person pronouns in this verse are singular, indicating Joshua is the addressee.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “For you will cause these people to inherit the land that I swore to their fathers to give to them.” The pronoun “them” at the end of the verse refers to either the people or to the fathers.

*Translator's note:* Or “Only be.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “so you can be careful to do.” The use of the infinitive לִשְׁמֹר (lishmor, “to keep”) after the imperatives suggests that strength and bravery will be necessary for obedience. Another option is to take the form לִשְׁמֹר as a vocative lamed (ל) with imperative (see {{Isaiah 38:20|Isa 38:20}} for an example of this construction), which could be translated, “Indeed, be careful!”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “commanded you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “be wise,” but the word can mean “be successful” by metonymy.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in all which you go.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “mouth.”

*Study note:* *This law scroll must not leave your lips*. The ancient practice of reading aloud to oneself as an aid to memorization is in view here.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “read it in undertones,” or “recite it quietly” (see *HALOT* 237 s.v. I הגה).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “be careful to do.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you will make your way prosperous.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and be wise,” but the word can mean “be successful” by metonymy.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Have I not commanded you?” The rhetorical question emphasizes the importance of the following command by reminding the listener that it is being repeated.

*Translator's note:* Or perhaps, “don’t get discouraged!”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in all which you go.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to enter to possess the land which the Lord your God is giving to you to possess it.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “remember the word which Moses, the Lord’s servant, commanded you.”

*Study note:* This command can be found in {{Deuteronomy 3:18|Deut 3:18-20}}. In vv. {{Joshua 1:13|13-15}} Joshua paraphrases the command, as the third person reference to Moses in v. {{Joshua 1:14|14}} indicates.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “is providing rest for you and is giving to you this land.”

*Study note:* “This land” refers to the trans-Jordanian lands allotted to these tribes.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “But you must cross over armed for battle before your brothers, all [you] mighty men of strength.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Then you may return to the land of your possession and possess it, that which Moses, the Lord’s servant, gave to you beyond the Jordan toward the rising of the sun.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “listened to.”

*Translator's note:* Or “Only.” Here and in v. {{Joshua 1:18|18}} this word qualifies what precedes (see also v. {{Joshua 1:7|7}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “any man who rebels against your mouth and does not listen to your words, to all which you command us, will be put to death.”

*Translator's note:* Or “Only.” Here and in v. {{Joshua 1:17|17}} this word qualifies what precedes (see also v. {{Joshua 1:7|7}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Joshua, son of Nun, sent from Shittim two men, spies, secretly, saying.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “go, see the land, and Jericho.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they went and entered the house of a woman, a prostitute, and her name was Rahab, and they slept there.”

*Translator's note:* Or “look.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “men have come here tonight from the sons of Israel.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the king of Jericho sent to Rahab, saying.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “bring out.”

*Translator's note:* The idiom “come to” (בוֹא אֶל, boʾ ʾel) probably has sexual connotations here, as it often does elsewhere when a man “comes to” a woman. If so, the phrase could be translated “your clients.” The instructions reflect Rahab’s perspective as to the identity of the men.

*Translator's note:* The words “the ones who came to your house” (*Heb* “who came to your house”) may be a euphemistic scribal addition designed to blur the sexual connotation of the preceding words.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “The woman took the two men and hid him.” The third masculine singular pronominal suffix on “hid” has to be a scribal error (see GKC §135.*p*).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the men came to me.” See the note on this phrase in v. {{Joshua 2:3|3}}.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “And the gate was to be shut in the darkness and the men went out.”

*Translator's note:* Another way to translate vv. {{Joshua 2:6|6-7}} would be, “While she took them up to the roof and hid them…, the king’s men tried to find them….” Both of the main clauses have the subject prior to the predicate, perhaps indicating simultaneous action. (On the grammatical point, see R. J. Williams, *Hebrew Syntax*, 42, §235.) In this case Rahab moves the Israelite spies from the hiding place referred to in v. {{Joshua 2:4|4}} to a safer and less accessible hiding place.

*Translator's note:* The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but is supplied for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “And the men chased after them [on] the road [leading to] the Jordan to the fords.” The text is written from the perspective of the king’s men. As far as they were concerned, they were chasing the spies.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “And they shut the gate after—as soon as the ones chasing after them went out.” The expressions “after” and “as soon as” may represent a conflation of alternate readings.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “she”; the referent (Rahab) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text adds, “to them.” This is somewhat redundant in English and has not been translated.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “has given the land to you.” Rahab’s statement uses the Hebrew perfect, suggesting certitude.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “terror of you has fallen upon us.”

*Translator's note:* Or “melting away because of.”

*Translator's note:* Both of these statements are actually subordinated to “I know” in the Hebrew text, which reads, “I know that the Lord…and that terror of you…and that all the inhabitants….”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and what you did to the two Amorite kings who were beyond the Jordan, Sihon and Og, how you annihilated them.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “And we heard and our heart[s] melted and there remained no longer breath in a man because of you.”

*Study note:* To swear an oath *in the Lord’s name* would make the Lord the witness and guarantor of the promise attached to the oath. If the person making the oath should go back on the promise, the Lord would judge him for breaking the contract.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Now, swear to me by the Lord.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “with the house of my father.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “true sign,” that is, “an inviolable token or pledge.”

*Translator's note:* The second person pronoun is masculine plural, indicating that Rahab’s entire family is in view.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Our lives in return for you to die.” If the lives of Rahab’s family are not spared, then the spies will pay for the broken vow with their own lives.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “If you do not report this matter of ours.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “allegiance and faithfulness.” These virtual synonyms are joined in the translation as “unswerving allegiance” to emphasize the degree of promised loyalty.

*Translator's note:* The second person pronoun is feminine singular, referring specifically to Rahab.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “she”; the referent (Rahab) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Text-critical note:* The phrase “by a rope” is omitted in the LXX. It may be a later clarifying addition. If original, the omission in the LXX is likely due to an error of homoioarcton. A scribe’s or translator’s eye could have jumped from the initial ב (bet) in the phrase בַּחֶבֶל (bakhevel, “with a rope”) to the initial ב on the immediately following בְּעַד (beʿad, “through”) and accidentally omitted the intervening letters.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “For her house.”

*Text-critical note:* These explanatory statements are omitted in the LXX and probably represent a later scribal addition.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Go.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “so that the pursuers might not meet you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the pursuers.” The object (“you”) is not in the Hebrew text but is implied.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “We are free from this oath of yours which you made us swear.” The words “unless the following conditions are met” are not in the Hebrew text, but are added for clarification.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Look! We are about to enter the land.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the cord of this red thread.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and your father and your mother and your brothers and all the house of your father gather to yourself to the house.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Anyone who goes out from the doors of your house to the outside, his blood is on his head. We are innocent.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “But anyone who is with you in the house, his blood is on our head if a hand should be on him.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and if you report this matter of ours.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the pursuers.” The object (“them”) is added for clarification.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the ones chasing them.” This has been rendered as “their pursuers” in the translation to avoid redundancy with the preceding clause.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “The pursuers looked in all the way and did not find [them].”
*Translator's note:* The words “the river,” though not in the Hebrew text, are added for clarification.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Surely the Lord has given into our hand all the land.” The report by the spies uses the Hebrew perfect, suggesting certitude.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “are melting away because of us.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “And Joshua arose early in the morning and he and the Israelites left Shittim and came to the Jordan.”

*Translator's note:* The words “the river,” though not in the Hebrew text, have been supplied in the translation for clarity.

*Study note:* The *ark of the covenant* refers to the wooden chest that symbolized God’s presence among his covenant people.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “set out from your place.”

*Translator's note:* Or “march.”

*Study note:* The precise distance is uncertain, but the measurement designated אַמָּה (ʾammah, “cubit”) was probably equivalent to approximately 18 inches, or 45 cm) in length.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “But there should be a distance between you and it, about 2,000 cubits in measurement.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “do not approach it.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “know.”
*Translator's note:* Or more literally, “to exalt you in the eyes of all Israel.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the edge of the waters of the Jordan.” The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “stand in the Jordan.” Here the repetition of the word “Jordan” would be redundant according to contemporary English style, so it was not included in the translation.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the soles of the feet.”

*Translator's note:* Or “Ruler”; or “Master.”

*Translator's note:* Or “rest in.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the waters of the Jordan, the waters descending from above, will be cut off so that they will stand in one pile.”
*Translator's note:* The verb, though not in the Hebrew, is added for clarification.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “dipped into the edge.”

*Study note:* The lengthy description of the priests’ arrival at the Jordan and the parenthetical reminder that the Jordan was at flood stage delay the climax of the story and add to its dramatic buildup.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the Jordan overflows all its banks all the days of harvest.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the waters descending from above stood still.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they stood in one pile very far away.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the [waters] descending… were completely cut off.”

*Study note:* The *Salt Sea* is an ancient name for the Dead Sea.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and all Israel was crossing over on dry ground until all the nation had finished crossing the Jordan.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “And when all the nation had finished crossing the Jordan.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “that this may be”; the referent of “this” (the 12 stones) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in order that this might be a sign among you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “were cut off from before.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “how the waters descending from above stood still.”
*Translator's note:* Here “also” has been supplied in the translation to make it clear (as indicated by v. {{Joshua 4:20|20}}) that these are not the same stones the men took from the river bed.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the presence of the people.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “men equipped for battle.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for war.”

*Study note:* The עֲרָבָה (ʿaravah, “rift valley”) extends from Galilee to the Gulf of Aqaba. The עַרְבוֹת (ʿarevot) of Jericho” refer to the parts of the Jordan Valley in the vicinity of Jericho (see *HALOT* 880 s.v. עֲרָבָה). The region is characterized by gently sloping plains which descend about 450 feet over the five miles from Jericho to the Jordan. Many translation say simply the “plains of Jericho” for the portion west of the Jordan and “plains of Moab” for the eastern portion. The translation here clarifies that the plains are part of the rift valley basin.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “feared.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all the days of his life.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “had feared.”

*Translator's note:* Traditionally, “the ark of the testimony,” another name for the ark of the covenant. The Hebrew term עֵדוּת (ʿedut, “testimony” or “witness”) here refers to the Mosaic covenant and the body of stipulations contained within it (see *HALOT* 791 s.v. 2).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the soles of the feet of the priests were brought up to the dry land.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the waters of the Jordan returned to their place and went as formerly over their banks.”

*Study note:* Verses {{Joshua 4:15|15-18}} give a more detailed account of the priests’ crossing that had been briefly described in v. {{Joshua 4:11|11}}.

*Study note:* The *first month* was the month Abib (= late March-early April in the modern calendar). The preparations for Passover also began on the tenth day of the first month ({{Exodus 12:2|Exod 12:2-3}}).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “these,” referring specifically to the 12 stones mentioned in vv. {{Joshua 4:3|3-7}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “make known to.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “crossed this Jordan”; the word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied to clarify the meaning.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “just as the Lord your God did to the Red Sea when he dried [it] up before us while we crossed over.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in order that.”

*Translator's note:* Or “peoples.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “know the hand of the Lord that it is strong.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “fear.”

*Text-critical note:* Another textual tradition has, “while we crossed.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “their heart[s] melted and there was no longer in them breath (or perhaps “spirit”) because of the sons of Israel.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “return, circumcise the sons of Israel a second time.” The Hebrew term שׁוּב (shuv, “return”) is used here in an adverbial sense to indicate the repetition of an action.

*Translator's note:* Or “Gibeath Haaraloth.” This name means “Hill of the Foreskins.” Many modern translations simply give the Hebrew name, although an explanatory note giving the meaning of the name is often included.

*Study note:* The name given to the place, *Hill of the Foreskins* was an obvious reminder of this important event.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “All the people who went out from Egypt, the males, all the men of war, died in the wilderness in the way when they went out from Egypt.”

*Translator's note:* Or “indeed.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “people.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all the people.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all the nation, the men of war who went out from Egypt, who did not listen to the voice of the Lord, came to an end.”

*Translator's note:* Some Hebrew mss, as well as the Syriac version, support this reading. Most ancient witnesses read “us.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “flowing with.”

*Study note:* The word picture *a land rich in milk and honey* depicts the land as containing many grazing areas (which would produce *milk*) and flowering plants (which would support the bees that produced *honey*).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “their sons he raised up in their place.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “rolled away.”

*Study note:* One might take *the disgrace of Egypt* as a reference to their uncircumcised condition (see {{Genesis 34:14|Gen 34:14}}), but the generation that left Egypt was circumcised (see v. {{Joshua 5:5|5}}). It more likely refers to the disgrace they experienced in Egyptian slavery. When this new generation reached the promised land and renewed their covenantal commitment to the Lord by submitting to the rite of circumcision, the Lord’s deliverance of his people from slavery, which had begun with the plagues and the crossing of the Red Sea, reached its climax. See T. C. Butler, *Joshua* (WBC), 59.

*Study note:* The name *Gilgal* sounds like the Hebrew verb “roll away” (גַּלַל, galal).
*Study note:* This is the area of the rift valley basin in the vicinity of Jericho (see the note at {{Joshua 4:13|Josh 4:13}}).
*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text adds, “on this same day.” This is somewhat redundant in English and has not been translated.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the day after, when they ate.” The present translation assumes this means the day after the Passover, though it is possible it refers to the day after they began eating the land’s produce.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the sons of Israel had no more manna.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he lifted up his eyes and looked. And look, a man was standing in front of him, and his sword was drawn in his hand.” The verb הִנֵּה (hinneh, “look”) invites the reader to view the scene through Joshua’s eyes. By calling the stranger “a man,” the author reflects Joshua’s perspective. The text shortly reveals his true identity (vv. {{Joshua 5:14|14-15}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Are you for us or for our enemies?”

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “He said, “Neither.” An alternative reading is לוֹ (lo, “[He said] to him”; cf. NEB). This reading is supported by many Hebrew mss, as well as the LXX and Syriac versions. The traditional reading of the MT (לֹא, loʾ, “no, neither”) is probably the product of aural confusion (the two variant readings sound the same in Hebrew). Although followed by a number of modern translations (cf. NIV, NRSV), this reading is problematic, for the commander of the Lord’s army would hardly have declared himself neutral.

*Study note:* The Lord’s heavenly army, like an earthly army, has a *commander* who leads the troops. For the phrase שַׂר־צְבָא (sar tsevaʾ, “army commander”) in the human sphere, see among many other references {{Genesis 21:22|Gen 21:22}}, {{Genesis 21:32|32}}; {{Genesis 26:26|26:26}}; {{Judges 4:2|Judg 4:2}}, {{Judges 4:7|7}}; {{1 Samuel 12:9|1 Sam 12:9}}.

*Study note:* The commander’s appearance seems to be for Joshua’s encouragement. Joshua could now lead Israel into battle knowing that the Lord’s invisible army would ensure victory.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Joshua fell on his face to the ground and bowed down.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “was shutting and shut up.” *HALOT* 743 s.v. I סגר paraphrases, “blocking [any way of access] and blocked [against any who would leave].”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “there was no one going out and there was no one coming in.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I have given into your hand Jericho.” The Hebrew verb נָתַתִּי (natatti, “I have given”) is probably best understood as a perfect of certitude, indicating the certainty of the action. The Hebrew pronominal suffix “your” is singular, being addressed to Joshua as the leader and representative of the nation. To convey to the modern reader what is about to happen and who is doing it, the translation “I am about to defeat Jericho for you” has been used.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and go around the city, all [you] men of war, encircling the city one time.” The Hebrew verb וְסַבֹּתֶם (vesabbotem, “and go around”) is plural, being addressed to the whole army.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and it will be at the sounding of the horn, the ram’s horn, when you hear the sound of the ram’s horn.” The text of {{Joshua 6:5|Josh 6:5}} seems to be unduly repetitive, so for the sake of English style and readability, it is best to streamline the text here. The reading in the Hebrew looks like a conflation of variant readings, with the second (“when you hear the sound of the ram’s horn”) being an interpolation that assimilates the text to verse {{Joshua 6:20|20}} (“when the army heard the sound of the horn”). Note that the words “when you hear the sound of the ram’s horn” do not appear in the LXX of verse {{Joshua 6:5|5}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all the people will shout with a loud shout.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “fall in its place.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the people will go up, each man straight ahead.”

*Translator's note:* An alternative reading is “and they said.” In this case the subject is indefinite and the verb should be translated as passive, “[the army] was told.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the people.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “pass by.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for the Lord has given to you the city.” The verbal form is a perfect, probably indicating certitude here.

*Translator's note:* Or “dedicated to the Lord.”

*Study note:* To make the city *set apart for the Lord* would involve annihilating all the people and animals and placing its riches in the Lord’s treasury (vv. {{Joshua 6:19|19}}, {{Joshua 6:21|21}}, {{Joshua 6:24|24}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “messengers.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Only you keep [away] from what is set apart [to God] so that you might not, as you are setting [it] apart, take some of what is set apart [to God] and turn the camp of Israel into what is set apart [to destruction by God] and bring trouble on it.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “it is holy to the Lord.”

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “and the people shouted and they blew the rams’ horns.” The initial statement (“and the people shouted”) seems premature, since the verse goes on to explain that the battle cry followed the blowing of the horns. The statement has probably been accidentally duplicated from what follows. It is omitted in the LXX.

*Study note:* The Negev is an area of central southern Judah, south of the hill country and west of the rift valley. As a geographic feature it is a depression extending south to the Gulf of Aqabah, but the biblical reference is probably to the northern portion of the region.

*Study note:* The foothills (שְׁפֵלָה, shephelah) are the transition region from the hill country to the Mediterranean coastal plains.

*Study note:* In contrast to the foothills on the western side of the hill country, the slopes are on the eastern side leading down to the rift valley of the Dead Sea and Jordan river.
